parole.testo: From Middle Low German abbedīe, from Old Saxon *abbadea, from Proto-West Germanic *abbadejā.
From Middle Low German acht, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtu (“attention”).

parole.significato: hornbeam, species in the genus Carpinus
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hagenboke (“garden beech”), from Old Saxon *heggia + bōkia, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju + *bōkijā. Compare German Hagebuche.
From Middle Low German bane, from Old Saxon *bana, from Proto-West Germanic *banu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *banō.

From Middle Low German barmhertich, originally a compound of arm (“poor”) + hert (“heart”) + -ich, from Proto-West Germanic *arm + *hertā + *-g, like German barmherzig, from Old High German armherz. In both branches of German, we have b- from the verb vorbarmen, erbarmen (“have mercy”) (hence Danish

From Middle Low German barsch, from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-West Germanic *bars, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“perch, bass”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórs-o-s, from *bʰers- (“top, tip, point”).
From Middle Low German bedrēgen, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan. Cognate with German betrügen, Dutch bedriegen.

parole.significato: to understand, to grasp, to fathom
parole.testo: From Middle Low German begrīpen, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrīpan. Equivalent to be- + gribe (“to grasp, gripe, seize”). Cognate to Swedish begripa and German begreifen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German behof, from Old Saxon *bihōf, from Proto-West Germanic *bihōf.
Borrowed from Middle Low German behôven, from Old Saxon *bihōvōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bihōfōn.
From Middle Low German beswīmen, from Old Saxon *swīman, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *swīman (“to sway, to swoon”).

parole.significato: to occupy (a space or a territory)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German besetten, from Old Saxon *bisettian, from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Proto-Germanic *bisatjaną (“to beset, set around”), cognate with German besetzen.

From Old Danish beletæ, from Middle Low German bilede, belde, from Old Saxon bilithi, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþi (“picture, image”), cognate with German Bild. Old Norse bilæti (“icon”) is also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German billich, from Proto-West Germanic *bilalīk. Compare German billig. Cognate with Old English bilewit.
From Middle Low German blank, from Old Saxon blank, from Proto-West Germanic *blank.

parole.significato: sheet metal (of any metal, e.g. aluminium or tin-coated iron)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bleck, from Old Saxon *blek, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką (“metal”).

From Old Danish borghæ, (late) Old Norse borga, possibly from Middle Low German borgen (“to vouch for”), from Old Saxon *borgōn, from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn. Cognate with Swedish borga (“to warrant”), English borrow, and German borgen (“to borrow”).
Possibly from Middle Low German bûgen, from Old Saxon būgan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan (“to bend”). Cognate with English bow, Dutch buigen, German biegen. Swedish buga is also from Low German.

From Middle Low German bocht, from Old Saxon *buht, from Proto-West Germanic *buhti, from Proto-Germanic *buhtiz (“bend, curve”). See also English bight, Icelandic bót (Swedish bukt and German Bucht are also borrowed from Low German). The noun is derived from the verb *beuganą (“to bend”).
From Middle Low German busse, from Old Saxon *buhsa, from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā.

From Middle Low German degelik (“prosperous, vigorous”), (from Old Saxon *dēg, from Proto-West Germanic *daig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz), + the suffix *-līkaz. Cognate with older Swedish dejlig, Norwegian Bokmål deilig and Dutch degelijk (“sound, solid”).

From Middle Low German dreien, from my Old Saxon thrāian, from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną, cognate with English throw, German drehen (“to turn”), Dutch draaien (“to turn”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German drîstich, from drîste + -ich, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī. By surface analysis, driste + -ig.
From Middle Low German drossel, from Old Saxon thrōsla, from Proto-West Germanic *þrostlā (“thrush”). Displaced native Danish trost (“thrush”).

From Middle Low German duchtig, from Old Saxon *duhtig, from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg, cognate with German tüchtig, Dutch duchtig, English doughty. Derived from the noun *duhti (“fitness”) (cf. German Tucht), a noun from the verb Proto-Germanic *duganą (“to be useful”), cf. Danish du.

From Old Danish dop, borrowed from Middle Low German dōpe, dōp, from Old Saxon dōpi, from Proto-West Germanic *daupīni (“immersion”), cognate with German Taufe, also whence Danish døbe (“to baptize”) and German taufen.
Probably from Middle Low German dōre, from Old Saxon *dōro, from Proto-West Germanic *dauʀō, cognate with German Tor and Dutch door. Late Old Norse dári is probably also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German effen, even (“even”), from Old Saxon evan, from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz (“even, level”). Related to jævn.
From Middle Low German valsch, from Old Saxon *falski, from Proto-West Germanic *falskī (“false, counterfeit”).

From Old Danish fastelaghen, borrowed from Middle Low German vastelāvent, vastāvent, a compound of vasten (“Lent”) + āvent (“evening”), the former from Old Saxon *fastōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fastēn (“to fast”). See also German Fastelovend (Cologne). Faroese føstulávint/fastalávint and Swedish

parole.significato: to understand or grasp the true meaning or significance of something.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vāten, from Old Saxon *fatōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną. Cognate with Swedish fatta, Norwegian Bokmål fatte, Dutch vatten and German fassen.

From Old Danish feet, from the neuter form of the adjective fed (“fat, obese”). It may also be a loan from or influenced by Middle Low German vet, from Old Saxon *fētid, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål fett, Norwegian Nynorsk feitt, Swedish fett.

From Old Danish feydhe, borrowed from Middle Low German veide, from Old Saxon *fēhitha, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“enmity, feud”). Cognate with English feud and German Fehde. It is an abstract noun derived from *faih (“hostile”) (cf. English foe).

From Old Danish feye, borrowed from Middle Low German vegen, from Old Saxon fegōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn. Cognate with Old High German vegōn, German fegen. Usually associated with Old Norse fága (“to adorn, polish”), Middle Low German vāgen, from Proto-Germanic *fēgōną, but the details are
From Middle Low German velt, from Old Saxon feld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu. Gender changed by influence from mark.
From Middle Low German vīle, from Old Saxon fila, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu.
From Middle Low German vlise, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *flint. Doublet of flint.

parole.significato: escape, flight (to get away from something)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vlucht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti (“flight”), cognate with English flight, German Flucht, Dutch vlucht. A conflation of two different nouns derived from two different verbs, *fleuhaną (“to flee”) and *fleuganą (“to fly”).

From Middle Low German vluchten, compare German flüchten. Derived from the noun Danish flugt, from Middle Low German vlucht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti (“flight”), cognate with English flight and German Flucht.
From Old Danish fald, from Middle Low German valde, from Old Saxon *faled, from Proto-West Germanic *falud.

From Middle Low German voracht, from Old Saxon, from Proto-West Germanic *firiahtu, from *firi- (“across, through”) + *ahtu (“attention, consideration”). Cognate with Swedish förakt, German Verachtung.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vörvelschen, vorvelschen, from Old Saxon *farfalskōn, from Proto-West Germanic *frafalskōn. By surface analysis, for- + falsk + -e. Cognate of Swedish förfalska.

parole.significato: to give up, forsake, abandon, renounce
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vorsaken, from Old Saxon farsakan, from Proto-West Germanic *frasakan.

for- + skrække. From Middle Low German vorschrecken (“to frighten”), from Old Saxon *firskrekkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fraskrekkōn, from *fra- + *skrekkōn (“to jump, skip”), possibly related to Proto-Germanic *skeraną (“to shear”) or *skrīaną (“to scream”). Also compare Old Norse skaga (“to jut

From Middle Low German vorsūmen (“to neglect, omit”). Derived from the verb sūmen (“to linger, delay”), säumen, from Old Saxon *sūmian, from Proto-West Germanic *sūmijan (“to let go”). Compare German versäumen, Dutch verzuimen.

Previously spelt frådse. From Middle Low German vrāsen, from Old Saxon fretan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraetan, cognate with German fressen (“to eat, devour”), English fret, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (fraitan, “to devour”). A compound of *fra- (“away”) + *etaną (“to eat”).

From Middle Low German vūcht (“moist; moisture”), from Old Saxon *fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht, cognate with German feucht (“moist”) (Norwegian fukt and Swedish fukt are also borrowed from Low German).

Equivalent to fugt (“moisture”) + -ig. From Middle Low German vuchtich (“moist”), derived from vucht (“moist, moisture”), from Old Saxon *fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht (cf. Danish fugt). Norwegian fuktig and Swedish fuktig are also borrowed from Low German.
From Middle Low German gaffel, gaffele, from Old Saxon gafala, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu (“fork”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German gābe, from Old Saxon *gāva, from Proto-West Germanic *gābā (“gift, giving”). Cognate with German Gabe. Late Old Norse gáfa and Swedish gåva are probably also from Low German. It has replaced a similar word with a different shape: Danish gæv (“feed”), from Old Norse gj

parole.significato: count (a nobleman, of the highest rank in Denmark, since 1849 without privileges; equivalent to a British earl)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grēve, from Old Saxon grāvio, from Proto-West Germanic *grāfijō.
From Middle Low German gunst, from Old Saxon unst, from Proto-West Germanic *unsti, from Proto-Germanic *undiz.

parole.significato: crowd, multitude (a large amount of people or animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hob, from Middle Low German hōp, from Old Saxon hōp, from Proto-West Germanic *haup (“heap”), cognate with English heap. Late Old Norse hópr and Swedish hop are also borrowed from Low German.

parole.significato: court (family and society of a sovereign)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hof, from Old Saxon hof, from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą, cognate with German Hof (“yard, court, farmyard”), Dutch hof (“yard, court, garden”), Old Norse hof (“shrine; court”). Doublet of hov (“shrine, temple”).
From Middle Low German hǖlen, from Old Saxon *hūwilon, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn.
From Middle Low German hōpen (“to hope”), from Old Saxon hopōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn.
From hån + -e, from Middle Low German hônen, from Old Saxon hōnian, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan. Compare Swedish håna.
From Middle Low German jagen (“to hunt”), from Old Saxon jagōn, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōn. Compare German jagen.
From Middle Low German kīken, from Old Saxon kīkan, from Proto-West Germanic *kīkan, cognate with Dutch kijken (Swedish kika and German kieken are also from Low German).
From Middle Low German klage, from Proto-West Germanic *klagu.
From Middle Low German klagen, from Proto-West Germanic *klagōn (“to lament, complain”).

parole.significato: a bluff; a cliff; a very steep incline at a coast
parole.testo: From Middle Low German klint, from Old Saxon *klint, from Proto-West Germanic *klint. Doublet of klit.

parole.significato: bedrock, rock; large, contiguous body of immobile stone
parole.testo: From Middle Low German klippe, related to klif (“cliff, rock”), from Old Saxon *klif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.
Borrowed from Middle Low German knecht, from Old Saxon kneht, from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.

From Middle Low German kôken, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn, an early loan from Late Latin cocō, from Classical Latin coquō (“to cook, roast”). Cognate with English cook, German kochen. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ-, whence also Sanskrit पचति (pacati), Russian печь (pečʹ).

From Old Danish kogher, from Middle Low German koker, from Proto-West Germanic *kokar, cognate with German Kocher, Dutch koker, Old English cocer (Swedish koger and Norwegian Bokmål kogger are borrowed, via Danish, from Low German). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür (“leather vessel f
From Middle Low German kort, from Old Saxon *kurt, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, cognate with German kurz, Dutch kort.
From Middle Low German kran, from krane (“crane (bird)”), from Old Saxon *krano, from Proto-West Germanic *kranō.

Borrowed and clipped from Middle Low German (büssen)krūt, (bussen)krût (“gunpowder”), from büsse (“rifle”) + krût (“spice, herb”), from Old Saxon krūd, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“herb, plant”). For the first element see Proto-West Germanic *buhsā.
From earlier kryde, from Middle Low German krǖden (“to season, spice”), from krût (“spice, herb”), from Old Saxon krūd, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“herb, plant”).
From Middle Low German krenken, from Old Saxon *krenkian, from Proto-West Germanic *krankijan.
Inherited from Old Danish korw, borrowed from Middle Low German korf, from Old Saxon *korf, from Proto-West Germanic *korb.
From Middle Low German kūsch, from Proto-West Germanic *kūski, cognate with German keusch, Dutch kuis, Old English cūsċ. Borrowed from Latin cōnscius (“conscious”).
From Middle Low German kempen, from Old Saxon kempio, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“battlefield”). Compare Swedish kämpa.

From Middle Low German kōpman, from Old Saxon kōpman, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupamann, cognate with English chapman and German Kaufmann. Equivalent to købe (“buy”) + mand (“man”). Possibly partially inherited from Old Norse kaupmaðr, the native parallel to the Low German.
From Middle Low German kȫken(e) (also as kȫke), from Old Saxon *kukina, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.
From Middle Low German lanksam, lanksum, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam (“lengthy, long-lasting”).

parole.significato: fief (a land given by a sovereign to a vassal in exchange for military services, especially in the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lēn, from Old Saxon lēhan, from Proto-West Germanic *laihn, from Proto-Germanic *laihną (“loan”), cognate with German Lehn (Swedish län is a loan from Low German). Doublet of lån.
Borrowed from Middle Low German lōt, from Old Saxon lōd, from Proto-West Germanic *laud, possibly borrowed from Gaulish *loudon, from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom (“lead”).
From Middle Low German los, from Old Saxon lohs, from Proto-West Germanic *luhs.

From Middle Low German luft, lucht (“air, smell”), from Old Saxon luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu. Probably influenced by German Luft (“air”). It is a cognate of Danish loft (“attic”) and Danish lugt (“smell”).

From Middle Low German lucht, luft (“air, smell”), from Old Saxon luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz. Cognate with German Luft (“air”) and Old Norse loft (“attic, air”) (whence Danish loft (“attic”)). Danish luft (“air”) is borrowed from the older form of the Low Germ
From Old Danish lyst, lust, from Middle Low German lust, from Old Saxon lust, from Proto-West Germanic *lustu. Cognate with English lust and German Lust. A different stem in Old Norse losti.

From Middle Low German māken, from Old Saxon makōn, from Proto-West Germanic *makōn, cognate with English make, German machen, Dutch maken. Old Norse maka, Norwegian make, Swedish maka are also borrowed from Low German. The verb is derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *makaz (“suitable”). A rat

From Middle Low German mālen (“to draw, paint”), from Old Saxon mālōn, from Proto-West Germanic *mālōn, from Proto-Germanic *mēlōną, which could be related to *mailą (“spot, blemish, mark”). Cognate with Icelandic mála (“to paint”).

parole.significato: marsh (low wet-land, from time to time flooded by the tide, especially with reference to the North Sea)
parole.testo: From Old Danish mersk, borrowed from Middle Low German marsch, mersch, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk, cognate with English marsh (Norwegian marsk and German Marsch are also from Low German). A compound from *mari (“sea”) + *-isk (“-ish”).

parole.significato: marshal (a military officer ranking over a general)
parole.testo: Older marskalk, borrowed from Middle Low German marschalk, from Old Saxon *marhskalk, from Proto-West Germanic *marhaskalk, from *marh (“horse”) + *skalk (“servant”). Cognate with German Marschall, Old High German marahscalc and borrowed to Old French mareschal (hence English marshal). The modern Da
Borrowed from Middle Low German mast, from Old Saxon *mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast.
From Middle Low German nachtegale, from Old Saxon nahtagala, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtigalā.
From Middle Low German neren, from Old Saxon nerian, from Proto-West Germanic *naʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *nazjaną (“to rescue, heal”), causative of *nesaną (“to survive, recover”).

From over (“over”) + sætte (“place, put, set”). From Middle Low German ȫversetten, ōversetten, from Old Saxon *ovarsettian, from Proto-West Germanic *ubarsattjan. Compare Swedish översätta and Norwegian Bokmål oversette.
From Middle Low German plicht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti (“care, duty”).
From Middle Low German proten (“to object, to grumble, to scold”), from Old Saxon *pratt, from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk”).

parole.significato: to concern, to be of (someone's) business
parole.testo: From Middle Low German rāken (“to hit, reach”), from Proto-West Germanic *rakōn. Probably related to the previous verb.

From rams + løg (“leek, onion”), borrowed from Middle Low German ramese (“ramson”), from Old Saxon *hramuso, from Proto-West Germanic *hramusō. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk ramslauk and Swedish ramslök. Cognates amoung non-Scandinavian languages are Lithuanian kermùšė (and šermukšnis), Russian чер
From Middle Low German reise, from Old Saxon *reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.
Borrowed from Middle Low German roder, from Old Saxon rōthar, from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr.

From Middle Low German rōf, from Old Saxon *rōf, from Proto-West Germanic *raub, from Proto-Germanic *raubaz (“pillage, booty”). Related to German Raub, Danish røv (“arse”) (from Proto-Germanic *raubō (“rift”)).
From Middle Low German rördum, the first element identical with rør (“reed”) and the second from Proto-West Germanic *dumil, an onomatopoeic root also found in Old English *dumbla (“bittern”).

From Middle Low German sāfte, sāchte, from Old Saxon *sāfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samft(ī) (compare Proto-Germanic *sōmiz (“agreeable, fitting”)), from Proto-Indo-European *sóm-tu-, possibly from *sem- (“one, whole”).
From Middle Low German sä̂lich, older form of sêlich, from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg (“happy, blissful”).

parole.significato: ointment (a thick viscous preparation for application to the skin, often containing medication)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German salve, from Old Saxon salva, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu.
From Middle Low German salven, from Old Saxon salbon, from Proto-West Germanic *salbōn (“to anoint”).
From Middle Low German sennep, from Old Saxon *senap, from Proto-West Germanic *senap, ultimately from Ancient Greek σίναπι (sínapi).
Borrowed from Middle Low German sichte, a variant of sicht, from Old Saxon *sihti, from Proto-West Germanic *sihti.
From Middle Low German seker, from Old Saxon sikur, sikor, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“free, secure”), from Latin sēcūrus (“secure, unworried”).
A borrowing from Middle Low German sin (“sense, perception, mind”), from Old Saxon *sinn, from Proto-West Germanic *sinn.
From Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą.

From Middle Low German schēn, from Old Saxon skehan, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan, from Proto-Germanic *skehaną (“to move quickly, emerge”). Cognate with German geschehen and Dutch geschieden. Norwegian skje and Swedish ske were also borrowed from Low German.
From Old Danish skoldær, from Middle Low German schulder, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldru. Cognate with English shoulder, German Schulter.
Possibly from Middle Low German schūwe, schū, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh. Compare English shy and German scheu.

parole.significato: to scold, nag (with the preposition på)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schenden, from Old Saxon *skendian, from Proto-West Germanic *skandijan.
From Middle Low German scherm, from Old Saxon *skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi. See also German Schirm; Icelandic skermur, Norwegian Bokmål skjerm, Swedish skärm are also from Low German.
From Middle Low German slūten (“to close”), from Old Saxon slūtan, from Proto-West Germanic *sleutan. Cognate with German schließen.
From Middle Low German slēpen, from Old Saxon *slēpian, from Proto-West Germanic *slaipijan, cognate with German schleifen (“to drag, slight”) (hence Danish sløjfe (“to demolish”)).
From Middle Low German smak, from Old Saxon *smakk, from Proto-West Germanic *smakku. Cognate with Dutch smaak, English smack, German Geschmack.
From Middle Low German smuk (“lithe, neat”), from Old Saxon *smuk, *smukk, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to crawl, creep”). Compare English smug and German schmuck (“pretty”).

parole.significato: to play (music, a game, in a theatrical performance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German spelen, from Old Saxon *spilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spilōn. Cognate with German spielen (Swedish spela is also from Low German).
From Middle Low German stempel, from the verb stampen, from Old Saxon *stampōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną (“to squeeze, compress”).
From Middle Low German stecken, from Old Saxon stekan, From Proto-West Germanic *stekan, from Proto-Germanic *stikaną.
From Middle Low German stille, from Old Saxon stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.

Formed from the verb straffe (“to penalize”), from Middle Low German straffen (“to punish, blame”), from Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”).

parole.significato: at once, immediately, straight away, right away, instantly
parole.testo: From Middle Low German strakes, strackes (“stretched, right away”), cognate with German stracks, Dutch straks (“later”). The Low German word was also borrowed to Norwegian straks, Swedish strax, Icelandic strax. The adverb is derived from the adjective Middle Low German strak (“straight”), German st
From Middle Low German streke, from Old Saxon *striki, from Proto-West Germanic *striki.
From Middle Low German stricken, from Old Saxon *striki, from Proto-West Germanic *striki. See also strække (“stretch”), streg (“line”), straks (“immediately”).

From Middle Low German strecken, from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan, cognate with English stretch, German strecken. Derived from the adjective *strakaz (“straight”). Compare streg (“line”), strikke (“knit”), straks (“immediately”).
From Middle Low German stump, from Old Saxon *stump, from Proto-West Germanic *stump, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz.
From Middle Low German störten, from Old Saxon *sturtian, from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan, cognate with German stürzen, English start, Dutch storten. Doublet of starte.
From Middle Low German stutten, from Old Saxon *stuttian, from Proto-West Germanic *stuttijan, cognate with German stützen.

From Middle Low German stȫven, from Old Saxon *stiovan, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan, cognate with German stauben (Swedish stöva is borrowed from Low German). A causative of the verb *steuban (“to smoke”).
From Middle Low German sunt, gesunt, from Proto-West Germanic *sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundaz, cf. also English sound and German gesund.
From Middle Low German swak, from Old Saxon *swak, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Compare with German schwach.
Borrowed from Middle Low German swinden, from Old Saxon swindan, from Proto-West Germanic *swindan.
From Middle Low German sēpe, from Old Saxon sēpa, from Proto-West Germanic *saipā, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.
From Middle Low German tacke, from Old Saxon *takko, from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”).
From Middle Low German talch, from Old Saxon *talg, from Proto-West Germanic *talg, from Proto-Germanic *talgaz.
From Middle Low German trechtäre, trechter, from Old Saxon trahtari, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī, from Late Latin tractārius, from Latin trāiectōrium.
Borrowed from Middle Low German trappe, from Old Saxon *trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.

From Middle Low German trecken, which is a merger of two related verbs: Old Saxon *trekkan and *trekkian, from Proto-West Germanic *trekan (“to push, drag”) and *trakkjan (“to drag”), cognate with Dutch trekken (hence English trek). Doublet of trekke.

From Middle Low German tüg (“tool, clothes”), from Old Saxon *tiug, from Proto-West Germanic *teug, from Proto-Germanic *teugą, *teugą, *tiugiją (“stuff, gear, device for pulling”). Cognates include English toy and German Zeug (“stuff, gear, fabric”).

parole.significato: to last, take (to have a certain duration)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wāren, from Proto-West Germanic *waʀōn, *weʀēn (“to stay, remain”), cognate with German währen. Derived from the verb *wesaną (“to be”) (Danish være).
From Middle Low German wēgeren, weigeren, from Proto-West Germanic *waigrōn (“to be stubborn”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German esel, from Old Saxon esil, from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Latin asellus. Largely replaced the inherited Old Norse asni.
